title: 22. Interview: Design E-commerce Platform
summary: Interview Q&A for Design E-commerce Platform — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design E-commerce Platform interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Step 6: Trade-offs & Interview Q&A (5 min)
sections.body:
### Trade-offs Discussed
- **Microservices vs monolith**: E-commerce at this scale needs microservices (independent scaling of search vs checkout vs catalog). But microservices add operational complexity (service mesh, distributed tracing). We use a hybrid: catalog/PDP as a single "browse" service (high read QPS, tight coupling) and checkout/order/payment as separate services (different consistency needs).
- **Redis vs DynamoDB for cart**: Redis is faster (sub-ms) but persistence is weaker; DynamoDB is durable but adds 5–10 ms latency. We use Redis with AOF persistence + async sync to Postgres.
- **Elasticsearch vs Postgres FTS**: ES gives better relevance tuning and facets; Postgres FTS is fine for small catalogs but doesn't scale to 100 M products with autocomplete.
- **GraphQL vs REST BFF**: GraphQL reduces over-fetching for mobile clients but adds complexity (N+1 queries, caching). We use REST BFFs for simplicity, with GraphQL only for the mobile app where payload size matters.
- **Eventual vs strong consistency for cart**: Eventually consistent (Redis → Postgres async) means a user logging in from a new device may see a stale cart for a few seconds — acceptable trade-off for sub-ms writes.

### Conceptual Interview Questions

### Q1. How do you prevent overselling during a flash sale with 100k concurrent buyers for the same SKU?
**Answer:** Overselling is the cardinal sin of e-commerce. We use a multi-layer defense: (1) **Atomic Redis Lua script** for inventory decrement — the script reads `available`, checks `available >= qty`, decrements, all in one atomic operation. No race condition possible within Redis. (2) **Per-warehouse sharding** — the SKU is stocked in 10 warehouses; each warehouse has its own Redis key (`inv:{sku}:{warehouse}`), so concurrent operations on different warehouses don't contend. Effective throughput: 10 keys × 10k ops/s = 100k ops/s. (3) **Pre-sale inventory reservation** — for announced flash sales, we pre-load inventory into Redis from Postgres, verify totals match, and disable the Postgres read path during the sale. (4) **Queue-based checkout** — for extreme cases (1 M concurrent), we put buyers in a virtual queue (CloudFront + Lambda@Edge hands out queue tokens); only N buyers per second reach checkout, matching inventory throughput. (5) **Final durable commit** — when the order is placed, we commit to Postgres with a transactional decrement; if the Redis count drifted (rare, due to crashes), reconciliation fixes it post-sale. Net result: zero overselling, but some buyers get "out of stock" even when Redis showed availability — they're refunded immediately if charged.
**Visual:**
```
buyer -> checkout -> Redis Lua (atomic):
   GET inv:{sku}:{wh}; if available >= qty: DECR available, INCR reserved
   else: reject "out of stock"
10 warehouses x 10k ops/s = 100k concurrent checkouts/s
extreme case: virtual queue (Lambda@Edge) throttles to inventory throughput
```

### Q2. How do you design search to return relevant results in 200 ms across 100 M products?
**Answer:** Elasticsearch is the core. (1) **Indexing**: each product is a document with `title`, `description`, `brand`, `category`, `attributes`, `price`, `rating`. We use analyzers per field (standard for description, keyword for brand, autocomplete for title). (2) **Sharding**: 30 primary shards × 2 replicas = 90 shards. Each shard holds ~3 M docs. A query fans out to all 30 primaries in parallel; results merge at coordinator. (3) **Relevance tuning**: BM25 scoring, with `title` boost (×3), `brand` boost (×2), `category` boost (×1.5). Synonym lists (`headphones ↔ earphones ↔ earbuds`). (4) **Facets**: ES aggregations on `brand`, `category`, `price_range`, `attributes.color` — computed in the same query, ~10 ms overhead. (5) **Caching**: top 10k searches cached in Redis for 60 s (hit rate ~40 % during peak). Autocomplete uses a smaller trie index in Redis (50 ms). (6) **Typo tolerance**: Levenshtein distance 2 on title field. (7) **Personalization**: post-ES, we re-rank top 100 results by user's recent views/purchases (collaborative filtering scores in Redis). (8) **Indexing lag**: CDC from Postgres → Kafka → ES sink; < 5 s lag for new products. (9) **Multi-region**: ES cluster per region; cross-region replication async for global catalog. (10) **Fallback**: if ES is down, Postgres trigram indexes serve the top 100k products (1 s latency, degraded banner).
**Visual:**
```
q="wireless headphones"
  -> Redis cache (60s) hit? return
  -> ES: 30 shards parallel
       BM25(title×3, brand×2, desc×1) + synonym expansion + Levenshtein-2
       + aggregations (brand, price, color)
  -> coordinator merges top 100
  -> personalization re-rank (Redis CF scores)
  -> return top 50 to user
p99 = 180ms
```

### Q3. How do you keep the product detail page fast at 600k QPS during Black Friday?
**Answer:** Three layers: (1) **CDN edge cache** — CloudFront caches the rendered PDP HTML for 60 s at the edge. Hit ratio ~70 % for popular products (long tail has lower hit rate). Edge cache absorbs the bulk of traffic. (2) **Origin shield** — a single CloudFront origin shield (e.g., us-east-1) collapses concurrent cache misses; if 1000 users request the same product within the same second, only one request reaches the origin. (3) **App-layer cache** — PDP Service checks Redis `pdp_cache:{product_id}` (JSON payload, 5 min TTL) before assembling. (4) **Read replicas** — Postgres has 10 read replicas; PDP reads from a random replica. (5) **Pre-warming** — before Black Friday, we pre-warm the CDN with the top 10k products via cache prefetch. (6) **Image strategy** — images served from a separate CDN (S3 + CloudFront) with 1-year TTL; image variants (thumbnail, medium, large) generated at upload time, not on-demand. (7) **GraphQL/REST composition** — PDP Service calls Catalog, Inventory, Review, Recommendation in parallel (Promise.all), assembling the response in ~50 ms when all caches hit. (8) **Stale-while-revalidate** — when the cache expires, serve stale while async-refreshing; user sees instant content, cache updates behind.
**Visual:**
```
user -> CloudFront edge (60s TTL) -> 70% hit
        -> origin shield (collapse misses) -> 95% hit
           -> PDP Service -> Redis pdp_cache (5min) -> 90% hit
              -> Postgres read replica (parallel: catalog, inv, review, reco)
              -> assemble JSON (50ms when all cache hit)
pre-warm top 10k products before peak
```

### Q4. How do you handle a price change between add-to-cart and checkout?
**Answer:** Three policies, merchant-configurable: (1) **Honor cart price** (default) — when the user adds to cart, we snapshot `unit_price` in the cart item. At checkout, we honor the snapshot price for 30 minutes (configurable). After 30 minutes, the cart refreshes prices. (2) **Honor current price** — cart shows current price; on checkout, the user pays current price. Simpler but bad UX (user added at $20, now $25). (3) **Notify on price change** — when seller changes price, we push a notification to users with the item in cart: "Price dropped to $18!" or "Price increased to $25." Our default is policy 1 (honor cart price) with a 30-minute snapshot window — balances UX (user gets the price they saw) with seller protection (no honoring week-old cart prices). For flash sales, sellers can set `cart_price_ttl=5min` to enforce the sale price strictly. Implementation: `cart_items.unit_price_snapshot` column; checkout reads snapshot if `added_at > now - 30min`, else refreshes from Catalog. Edge case: if the product is now discontinued or out of stock, we refuse checkout with a clear message.
**Visual:**
```
add to cart: cart_items.unit_price_snapshot = $20 (added_at = T0)
checkout at T0+10min: use snapshot $20
checkout at T0+40min: refresh -> current price $25 (notify user)
seller config: cart_price_ttl = 30min (default) or 5min (flash sale)
```

### Q5. How do you build recommendations for 100 M users without real-time computation?
**Answer:** We pre-compute recommendations offline and serve them from Redis. (1) **Data sources** — user behavior events (view, cart-add, purchase, rating) streamed via Kafka to S3, then loaded into Spark nightly. (2) **Collaborative filtering** — ALS (Alternating Least Squares) matrix factorization on the user × product interaction matrix. Trains on the last 30 days of behavior; produces a 64-dim embedding per user and per product. (3) **Top-N per user** — for each user, compute dot-product scores against all products, take top 50, write to Redis `reco:{user_id}` as a sorted set. (4) **Content-based fallback** — for new users (no history), recommend top-selling products in their geo / category affinity inferred from signup. (5) **Real-time signals** — when a user views a product, we re-rank the pre-computed list with "customers also viewed for this product" (a pre-computed product-to-product similarity map). (6) **Context** — home page (general recommendations), PDP ("frequently bought together"), cart ("complete your cart"). Each context has its own pre-computed set. (7) **Cold-start for products** — new products have no interactions; we use content features (category, brand, attributes) to match them to similar products' audiences. (8) **Refresh cadence** — nightly batch; for power users (>50 events/day), refresh every 4 hours. (9) **A/B testing** — 1 % of users get experimental models; CTR and conversion rate measured over 2 weeks before rollout. Redis cost: 100 M users × 50 recs × 16 bytes ≈ 80 GB — fits in 3 Redis shards.
**Visual:**
```
nightly Spark job:
  Kafka events (30d) -> S3 -> ALS matrix factorization
  -> 64-dim embeddings per user, per product
  -> for each user: dot-product with all products -> top 50
  -> write to Redis reco:{user_id} (ZSET)
real-time: PDP view -> re-rank with product-to-product similarity
cold start: new user -> geo top-sellers; new product -> content-based match
refresh: nightly (normal), 4h (power users)
```

### Q6. How do you ensure the order placement is exactly-once (no duplicate orders)?
**Answer:** Exactly-once across distributed systems is hard; we use idempotency + at-least-once delivery = effectively-once. (1) **Idempotency key** — the client generates a UUID `idempotency_key` for the "place order" intent; it's stored in `orders.idempotency_key` with a unique constraint. (2) **Idempotency cache** — Redis `idem:order:{user_id}:{idem_key}` caches the response (order_id or failure) for 24 h. Retries within 24 h return the cached response without re-processing. (3) **Database unique constraint** — `UNIQUE(user_id, idempotency_key)` on the orders table; even if the Redis cache misses (e.g., expired) and two retries race, only one INSERT succeeds; the other gets a unique-violation and the service reads the existing order. (4) **Payment idempotency** — the same `idempotency_key` is passed to the Payment Gateway, so retries don't double-charge. (5) **Inventory idempotency** — the `checkout_id` (tied to the idempotency key) holds the inventory reservation; commit is idempotent (a flag `committed=true` prevents double-decrement). (6) **Client contract** — the client MUST retry with the same `idempotency_key` on timeout/network failure; if it generates a new key, we treat it as a new intent (potential duplicate, but that's the client's bug). (7) **Monitoring** — alert on `duplicate_order_attempts` metric (attempts where idempotency cache hit); a spike indicates clients are retrying heavily (possibly due to slow checkout).
**Visual:**
```
client POST /checkout/{id}/place (idempotency_key=K)
  -> Redis idem:order:u:K hit? return cached
  -> Redis SET NX lock:order:u:K (10 min)
  -> INSERT orders (... idempotency_key=K) UNIQUE(user_id, K)
       -> unique violation? SELECT existing order, return it
  -> Payment.capture(idempotency_key=K) -> Payment Gateway idempotent
  -> Inventory.commit(checkout_id) -> idempotent flag
  -> cache response (24h)
  -> return {order_id}
```

### Q7. How do you handle returns and refunds without breaking inventory or accounting?
**Answer:** Returns have their own state machine: `requested → approved → shipped_back → received → refunded → closed`. (1) **Return request** — user initiates via order history; creates a `returns` row with `status=requested`, lists items + reasons. (2) **Seller approval** — seller reviews; if approved, sends a return shipping label (carrier API integration). (3) **Item shipped back** — user ships; carrier webhook updates tracking. (4) **Warehouse receipt** — when the item arrives at the warehouse, warehouse staff inspects and marks `received`. (5) **Refund** — `POST /v1/orders/{id}/refund` to Payment Service → Payment Gateway refund (idempotent, full or partial). Order status updates to `returned`. (6) **Inventory restock** — Inventory Service increments `stock_qty` for the returned items (and `available` in Redis); items may be marked `open_box` for resale at discount. (7) **Accounting** — settlement adjustments: the original settlement is reversed (a `settlement_adjustment` row), reducing the next payout to the seller. (8) **Restocking fee** — if applicable, deducted from refund (configurable per category). (9) **Return fraud** — high return-rate users flagged for review; serial returners limited (e.g., max 5 returns/month). (10) **Analytics** — return rate per product/category/seller monitored; high return rate (> 20 %) triggers product quality review.
**Visual:**
```
return lifecycle:
  user -> POST /returns (items, reasons) -> returns.status=requested
  seller approves -> send label -> status=approved
  user ships -> carrier webhook -> status=shipped_back
  warehouse receives -> status=received
  refund -> Payment Gateway (idempotent) -> status=refunded
  inventory: stock_qty += returned, available += returned (Redis + Postgres)
  accounting: settlement_adjustment -= refund_amount (next payout reduced)
  order status -> returned
  fraud: high return rate user flagged
```

### Scenario-Based Interview Questions

### Q1. A flash sale for a viral product starts in 5 minutes. Expected 1 M concurrent users. What do you do RIGHT NOW?
**Answer:** Triage in priority order: (1) **Pre-warm inventory** — load the SKU's stock count into Redis from Postgres; verify counts match; lock the Postgres write path (sales use Redis only). (2) **Pre-warm CDN** — cache the PDP HTML at edge for the product; pre-generate image variants. (3) **Scale checkout** — auto-scale Checkout Service to 5× current; pre-warm Kafka partitions. (4) **Virtual queue** — enable CloudFront + Lambda@Edge queue: each buyer gets a queue position; only 10 k buyers/sec proceed to checkout (matching Redis throughput). Others see "You are in queue, position 5432, est 8 min." (5) **Disable non-essential** — disable recommendations and reviews on the PDP (static fallback); disable "customers also bought." (6) **Rate-limit search** — the product name will be heavily searched; cache the search result in Redis for 5 min. (7) **Payment capacity** — pre-warm Payment Gateway connection pool; alert the gateway provider (Stripe) of expected volume; consider backup gateway. (8) **Database protection** — read-only mode for Postgres read replicas; only the order-write primary takes writes, and it's pre-scaled. (9) **Monitoring** — dashboard with key metrics (checkout latency, error rate, inventory remaining, queue length); on-call team in war room. (10) **Communication** — status page; in-app banner acknowledging high traffic. (11) **Rollback plan** — if checkout starts failing > 1 %, pause new checkouts (show "sale paused, retry in 5 min"), preserve in-flight orders.
**Visual:**
```
T-5min:
  pre-warm: CDN PDP, Redis inventory, Kafka partitions
  scale: Checkout 5x, Payment pool, Postgres primary
  enable: virtual queue (Lambda@Edge), 10k/s checkout cap
  disable: recommendations, reviews on PDP (static fallback)
  cache: search result 5min
  monitor: latency, errors, inventory, queue length
  war room: on-call team
```

### Q2. A seller uploads a CSV with 1 M product updates (price changes). How do you process this without overwhelming the system?
**Answer:** (1) **Async batch ingest** — the seller's CSV upload goes to S3 via pre-signed URL; seller gets `batch_id` immediately. (2) **Queue processing** — an SQS/Kafka job per batch; worker reads CSV in chunks of 1000 rows. (3) **Rate limiting** — cap updates at 10 k/s globally to avoid overwhelming Postgres or ES reindexing. (4) **Postgres bulk upsert** — `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (product_id) DO UPDATE` with batches of 1000 rows; uses a single transaction per batch. (5) **CDC to Elasticsearch** — Postgres → Debezium → Kafka → ES sink; the ES sink batches at 5 k/s to avoid overloading the cluster. (6) **Cache invalidation** — for each updated product, publish to Redis pub/sub `product_updated` channel; PDP and price caches are invalidated. (7) **Idempotency** — if the seller re-uploads the same CSV, the `batch_id` dedupes (rows already updated are skipped based on `updated_at` comparison). (8) **Progress tracking** — `batches` table tracks `total_rows, processed_rows, failed_rows`; seller sees progress in portal. (9) **Error handling** — invalid rows (bad SKU, missing fields) written to an `errors.csv` in S3; seller downloads, fixes, re-uploads. (10) **Notification** — seller gets email when batch completes. (11) **Time window** — large batches scheduled for off-peak hours (2 AM local) to minimize customer impact. (12) **Rollback** — for price changes, we keep the prior price for 24 h in case of seller error; `products.previous_price` column.
**Visual:**
```
seller uploads CSV -> S3 -> batch_id
worker (SQS job) reads CSV in 1000-row chunks
  -> Postgres bulk upsert (1000/tx) at 10k/s global cap
  -> Debezium CDC -> Kafka -> ES sink (5k/s batch)
  -> Redis pub/sub product_updated -> invalidate PDP + price cache
progress: batches table (total/processed/failed)
errors: bad rows -> errors.csv -> seller re-uploads
email seller on completion
```

### Q3. Users report that "Add to Cart" is sometimes showing the wrong price after a few minutes. Diagnose.
**Answer:** Likely a cache staleness issue. Investigation: (1) **Reproduce** — add an item, watch the price for 5 minutes; does it change? Capture the price at each step (add to cart, view cart, checkout). (2) **Check the price cache** — `price:{sku_id}` in Redis; what's the TTL? If 5 min, the cache expires and the next read fetches from Postgres (which may have a new price). (3) **Check the cart snapshot logic** — does the cart store `unit_price_snapshot`? If not, every cart read fetches current price — wrong behavior (should snapshot at add-time for 30 min). (4) **Check for seller price changes** — query `products` for `updated_at` in the last hour; if many SKUs changed, the cart is correctly reflecting the new price but UX is jarring. (5) **Check multi-device sync** — if the user has two devices, the second device may fetch the cart from Postgres (async sync lag) and see a different price than the first. Fix: (a) **Enforce cart price snapshot** — `cart_items.unit_price_snapshot` set at add time; cart display uses snapshot for 30 min, then refreshes. (b) **Stale-while-revalidate for price cache** — when TTL expires, serve stale while async-refreshing; never show a "new" price without user action. (c) **Price-change notification** — when seller changes price, push a notification to all carts containing the SKU: "Price changed from $20 to $18" or "$25". (d) **Atomic snapshot** — when adding to cart, use the price visible in the PDP at that moment (which the user saw); pass it from the client as `client_seen_price` and verify against backend within ±$0.01 (allowing for rounding).
**Visual:**
```
diagnosis:
 1. capture price at: PDP view, add-to-cart, view-cart, checkout
 2. price:{sku} Redis TTL (5min?) -> expiry causes refresh
 3. cart_items.unit_price_snapshot set at add-time?
 4. multi-device sync lag (Postgres async)
fix:
 - cart snapshot for 30 min, then refresh
 - stale-while-revalidate on price cache
 - notify on price change to active carts
 - client_seen_price verification
```

### Q4. The recommendation model is producing bizarre suggestions (users seeing baby products when they have no children). How do you debug?
**Answer:** (1) **Identify the affected users** — pull a sample of 100 users reporting bad recs; query their `reco:{user_id}` from Redis. (2) **Check the input data** — for each affected user, pull their behavior events from the last 30 days (Kafka → S3 → Spark input). Look for: any baby-product views/purchases? Often the issue is one mis-categorized event (e.g., the user bought a gift). (3) **Check the model** — the ALS model produces user and product embeddings; cosine similarity between the affected user's embedding and the baby-product embeddings. If high, the model genuinely learned this association — it's not a bug, it's a feature (the user might be a gift-buyer). (4) **Check the candidate generation** — did the baby products enter the candidate set via a different path (e.g., "trending in your region" or "popular this week")? Real-time signals can override offline recs. (5) **Check for data quality** — were events mis-attributed? (e.g., shared account, cookie bleed across users). Check the user_id mapping; sometimes a session_id gets re-used. (6) **Check the deployment** — was a new model version deployed recently? Compare recs before and after. (7) **Feedback loop** — add a "not relevant" button on recs; users who downvote baby products get a `negative_signal` that suppresses similar recs. (8) **Category exclusion** — let users explicitly exclude categories ("don't show me baby products"). (9) **Guardrails** — top-level rule: don't show category X to users with no history in category X (configurable per category). (10) **A/B test** — the new model with guardrails vs old model; measure CTR and "not relevant" downvotes.
**Visual:**
```
debug:
 1. sample 100 affected users -> Redis reco:{user_id}
 2. pull 30d behavior (Kafka->S3->Spark input) -> any baby-product events?
 3. ALS embeddings: cosine(user, baby_product) high? learned or bug?
 4. candidate paths: trending/regional override offline?
 5. data quality: shared account, cookie bleed, session reuse
 6. deployment diff: model version change?
fix:
 - "not relevant" feedback button -> negative signal
 - category exclusion user setting
 - guardrail rule: no category X without history in X
 - A/B test guardrails vs current
```

### Q5. Cyber Monday: the search cluster is at 90 % CPU and latency is creeping up. What do you do?
**Answer:** Immediate actions (next 5 minutes): (1) **Scale ES** — add 10 more data nodes; ES auto-rebalances shards (takes 10–30 min, but immediate relief once shards relocate). (2) **Increase cache TTL** — bump search-result Redis cache from 60 s to 300 s; sacrifices freshness for throughput. (3) **Reduce facet computation** — disable the least-used facets (e.g., "seller" facet) to save aggregation time. (4) **Throttle slow queries** — queries taking > 500 ms get cancelled (`search.cancel` API); user sees "results loading, please retry." (5) **Shed load** — for non-essential pages (e.g., "browse all categories"), return cached static results instead of hitting ES. (6) **Read replicas** — route read queries to the replica shards (already 2× replicated, but ensure coordinator prefers replicas). (7) **Index optimization** — ensure `index.refresh_interval` is bumped from 1s to 30s during peak (sacrifices indexing freshness for search throughput). (8) **Circuit breaker** — if ES latency exceeds 1 s, fall back to Postgres trigram search for the top 100k products; show degraded banner. (9) **Post-incident** — provision for 2× next year's expected peak; consider OpenSearch's search-async mode for high QPS; tune shard count (current 30 may be too few for 200k QPS).
**Visual:**
```
immediate (T+5min):
  scale ES +10 data nodes (rebalance)
  cache TTL 60s -> 300s
  disable low-value facets
  cancel queries >500ms
  static cache for non-essential browse pages
  prefer replica shards for reads
  refresh_interval 1s -> 30s
if latency >1s:
  fallback to Postgres trigram (top 100k products, degraded banner)
post-incident:
  provision 2x next year's peak
```

### Q6. A new seller wants to bulk-upload 50k products but most have missing required attributes. How do you handle?
**Answer:** (1) **Validate at upload** — the Catalog API enforces required fields (title, price, category, brand, at least 1 image). Invalid rows go to an `errors.csv` with reasons. (2) **Schema-per-category** — different categories have different required attributes (e.g., electronics requires `warranty_months`, apparel requires `size_chart`). The seller's CSV must match the category template. (3) **Template download** — seller downloads a category-specific CSV template with headers and example rows; validated client-side before upload. (4) **Partial acceptance** — accept the rows that pass validation; reject the rest. Seller sees "45,000 of 50,000 accepted; 5,000 rejected (download errors.csv)." (5) **Auto-fill from attributes** — if `color` is missing but the title contains "Red", we suggest "Red" as the color (AI-assisted attribute extraction). Seller confirms. (6) **Bulk edit** — seller portal has a bulk-edit UI to fix common issues (e.g., set `brand=X` for all rejected rows). (7) **Image requirement** — products without images are accepted but `is_active=false` (not visible to buyers) until images are uploaded. (8) **Staged review** — for new sellers, the first 100 products go through manual review (moderation for prohibited items, brand-counterfeit check); after approval, bulk uploads proceed without review. (9) **Attribute inference** — for products with sparse attributes, our catalog enrichment service (nightly Spark job) infers attributes from description, title, and similar products. (10) **Catalog quality score** — each product gets a completeness score (0–100); products below 50 are deprioritized in search.
**Visual:**
```
seller uploads 50k CSV
  -> validate per-row against category schema
  -> 45k pass -> INSERT (active=true if images present, false otherwise)
  -> 5k fail -> errors.csv (row, reason)
seller fixes via:
  - bulk-edit UI (set brand=X for all rejected)
  - re-upload errors.csv
AI assist: extract color/size from title -> suggest -> seller confirms
catalog enrichment: nightly Spark infers missing attributes from description
quality score: <50 -> deprioritize in search
```

### Q7. Customers are abandoning carts at checkout due to slow shipping address validation. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** (1) **Diagnose** — measure: where is the latency? Address autocomplete (geocoding API)? Address validation (USPS/Google)? Tax calculation? Shipping quote (carrier API)? Each is a separate call; serial execution adds up. (2) **Address autocomplete** — use a CDN-cached geocoding service (Google Places, Mapbox, HERE); cache top 10k city/postal-code lookups in Redis; pre-fetch when user types 3+ chars. (3) **Address validation** — debounce: don't validate on every keystroke; validate on field blur or "Continue" click. (4) **Tax calculation** — pre-compute tax rates per postal code (monthly refresh from a tax provider like TaxJar/Avalara); cache in Redis. Lookup is sub-ms. (5) **Shipping quote** — carrier APIs are slow (1–3 s); pre-negotiated rates cached per `(origin_warehouse, destination_postal_code, weight_bucket)`; refresh weekly. Real-time quote only for unusual weights/sizes. (6) **Parallel calls** — when the user clicks "Continue to shipping," fire address validation + tax + shipping quote in parallel (Promise.all), not serial. Total latency = max(component latencies) instead of sum. (7) **Optimistic UI** — show estimated shipping/tax while the call is in flight; update when results arrive. User doesn't wait staring at a spinner. (8) **Pre-compute on cart view** — when the user opens the cart, pre-fetch shipping/tax for their default address (most users have one). (9) **Cache per session** — once calculated for an address, cache for 30 minutes (rates don't change). (10) **Fallback** — if a carrier API is slow (>2 s), show "Calculated at checkout" and let the user proceed; finalize when the API responds.
**Visual:**
```
diagnosis: address-autocomplete + validation + tax + shipping (serial = 5s)
fix:
 - autocomplete: CDN-cached geocoding, pre-fetch at 3 chars
 - validation: on blur, not keystroke
 - tax: pre-computed per postal code (monthly refresh), Redis cache
 - shipping: cached per (origin, dest, weight bucket), weekly refresh
 - parallel: Promise.all(validation, tax, shipping) -> max latency
 - optimistic UI: show estimates, update on response
 - pre-fetch on cart view for default address
 - session cache 30min
 - fallback: "calculated at checkout" if carrier >2s
```
